sections.title: Introduction to Electrostatics
sections.narration: Welcome! Have you ever wondered what causes a spark when you touch a doorknob, or why a balloon sticks to the wall after you rub it on your hair? The answer lies in the fascinating world of electricity. At its very core, electricity is all about a fundamental property of matter called charge. In this chapter, we begin our journey into classical electricity by exploring electrostatics. This is the study of charges that are not moving, or are 'static'. We'll discover the forces they exert on each other, the fields they create, and the energy stored within these arrangements. We will also touch upon how this differs from electric currents, which involve moving charges, and electromagnetism, which studies the interplay between moving charges and magnetic fields. So, get ready to dive deep into the invisible world of static charges and the powerful forces that govern our universe.

sections.title: Chapter Summary
sections.narration: Let's quickly summarize what we've learned. We started with the fundamental concept of electric charge, which comes in two types: positive and negative. We established that charge is conserved, meaning it cannot be created or destroyed, and quantized, existing in discrete packets of the elementary charge 'e'. We explored methods of charging, including friction, conduction, and induction. A key highlight was Coulomb's Law, which mathematically describes the force between two point charges, showing it's proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. We saw how this force changes in a medium with a dielectric constant. We also learned how to use the vector form of Coulomb's Law and the superposition principle to calculate the net force on a charge from multiple other charges. Finally, we defined electrostatic equilibrium as the state where the net force on a charge is zero, and analyzed conditions for stable and unstable equilibrium.

sections.title: The Fundamental Concept of Charge
sections.narration: Let's dive into the core concept: electric charge. Think of the fundamental building blocks of matter: atoms. Normally, an atom is electrically neutral, because it contains an equal number of positively charged protons in its nucleus and negatively charged electrons orbiting that nucleus. The positive charge of a proton and the negative charge of an electron are equal in magnitude, creating a perfect balance. The charge on a single electron or a single proton is the smallest unit of free charge we've ever discovered. But how do objects become charged? It's all about the movement of electrons. We can't easily add or remove protons, as they are bound tightly in the nucleus. Electrons, however, are on the outside and can be transferred. If an object gains extra electrons, it now has more negative charges than positive charges, and we say it is negatively charged. Conversely, if an object loses some of its electrons, the balance is tipped. It now has more positive protons than negative electrons, and we call it positively charged. These simple labels, positive and negative, were first assigned by the American scientist and inventor, Benjamin Franklin. This fundamental idea—that charging is simply the transfer of electrons—is the key to understanding all of electrostatics.

sections.title: Basic Properties of Electric Charge
sections.narration: Now that we understand what charge is, let's explore its fundamental properties. First, charge is a scalar quantity, much like mass or temperature. This means it only has magnitude, not direction. And as we know, it comes in two types, positive and negative. When we combine charges, they add up algebraically. For instance, if you have a charge of +3 units and you add a charge of -1 unit, the net charge is simply +2 units. Second, and crucially, charge is conserved. This is a fundamental law of physics. In any isolated system, the net electric charge remains constant, no matter what process takes place. It can be a chemical reaction, a nuclear decay, or any other interaction. Charge can be moved around, or positive and negative charges can be created in pairs, but the total amount of charge never changes. It is never created from nothing or destroyed into nothing. For example, in radioactive decay, like a Uranium-238 atom decaying into Thorium and an alpha particle, the total charge before and after the decay is exactly the same. Similarly, in exotic processes like annihilation, where an electron and its antimatter counterpart, a positron, collide, the total charge is zero before and zero after. The same conservation holds true for pair production, where energy converts into an electron-positron pair.

sections.title: Quantization of Charge
sections.narration: The third fundamental property of charge is that it is quantized. This might sound complex, but the idea is simple. It means that electric charge doesn't come in any arbitrary amount; it exists in discrete packets. This was a groundbreaking discovery by Robert Millikan through his famous oil drop experiment. He found that the charge on any object is always an integer multiple of a fundamental unit of charge, which we denote by 'e'. This is the magnitude of the charge of a single electron. The formula for this principle is q equals N times e, where 'q' is the total charge, 'e' is the fundamental charge, and 'N' must be an integer—like 1, 2, 3, or -1, -2, -3. This means an object can have a charge of 2e or -10e, but it can never have a charge of, say, one-third of 'e' or 2.5 times 'e'. This is because charging happens by transferring whole electrons; you can't transfer half an electron. Now, you might have heard of quarks, which are fundamental particles that make up protons and neutrons. Physicists have discovered that quarks can have fractional charges, like plus or minus e/3 or 2e/3. However, quarks are not stable in a free state; they are always bound together inside larger particles. Therefore, for all practical purposes and when dealing with free charges, the smallest unit of charge that can be added or removed is 'e', the charge of a single electron.

sections.title: Further Properties of Charge
sections.narration: Let's cover a few more essential properties of electric charge. First, as you've likely experienced with magnets, similar charges repel each other, while opposite charges attract. Two positive charges will push each other away, as will two negative charges. But a positive and a negative charge will pull towards each other. It’s important to note, however, that the definitive test for whether an object is charged—what we call the true test of electrification—is repulsion, not attraction. Why? Because attraction can also occur between a charged body and a neutral, uncharged body due to a phenomenon called induction, which we will explore later. Repulsion, however, only happens between two bodies with like charges. Another property is that charge is always associated with mass. A particle must have mass to carry a charge. The reverse is not true; a particle like a neutron has mass but no charge. When an object becomes negatively charged by gaining electrons, its mass slightly increases. When it becomes positively charged by losing electrons, its mass slightly decreases, although this change is usually incredibly small. Additionally, charge is transferable. It can move from one object to another upon contact, a process known as conduction. Charge is also invariant, meaning its value doesn't change regardless of how fast you're moving. A charge of 1 coulomb is 1 coulomb whether you are standing still or on a rocket ship. Finally, a charge's motion dictates the fields it produces. A stationary charge creates only an electric field. A charge moving at a constant velocity creates both an electric and a magnetic field. And an accelerating charge not only creates both fields but also radiates energy in the form of electromagnetic waves.

When an object becomes negatively charged by gaining electrons, its mass slightly increases. When it becomes positively charged by losing electrons, its mass slightly decreases, although this change is usually incredibly small.

Additionally, charge is transferable... Charge is also invariant... Finally, a charge's motion dictates the fields it produces. A stationary charge creates only an electric field. A charge moving at a constant velocity creates both an electric and a magnetic field. And an accelerating charge...radiates energy...

sections.title: Units of Charge
sections.narration: To work with charge quantitatively, we need a consistent unit of measurement. The standard international, or SI, unit for electric charge is the coulomb, symbolized by a capital 'C'. But what exactly is one coulomb? It's a very large amount of charge. To understand its scale, we can relate it to electric current, which is the flow of charge over time. The unit for current is the ampere (A). The relationship is given by the simple formula: charge equals current multiplied by time, or q = I times t. From this, we can define one coulomb as the amount of charge that flows past a point in a conductor in one second when the current is one ampere. So, one coulomb is equal to one ampere-second. To give you some perspective, the charge of a single electron is incredibly small, just negative 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 19 coulombs. This means you would need about 6.25 quintillion electrons to make up a charge of just negative one coulomb! Besides the coulomb, there are other units. In the CGS system, we have the electrostatic unit or 'esu', also known as the statcoulomb or frankline. One coulomb is equivalent to 3 times 10 to the power of 9 esu. For practical applications, especially in electronics and battery capacity, you might see units like the ampere-hour, which is equal to 3600 coulombs, or the faraday, a unit used in chemistry, which is about 96,500 coulombs.

sections.title: Methods of Charging: Triboelectricity
sections.narration: So, how do we actually get objects to be charged? There are several methods, and the most common one you've experienced is charging by friction, also known as triboelectricity. This happens when you rub two different materials together, like a glass rod with a silk cloth, or your hair with a plastic comb. It’s a common misconception that the rubbing process 'creates' charge. This is not true. The rubbing simply provides the energy needed to transfer electrons that are already present in the materials from one surface to another. Remember, charge is conserved! No new electrons or protons are created. Certain materials have a tendency to give up electrons, while others have a tendency to accept them. We can organize materials into a 'triboelectric series'. When you rub any two materials from this series together, the one that appears earlier in the list will become positively charged (by losing electrons), and the one that appears later will become negatively charged (by gaining electrons). For example, if you rub a glass rod with a silk cloth, glass loses electrons to the silk. The glass rod becomes electron-deficient and thus positively charged, while the silk cloth now has an excess of electrons and becomes negatively charged. This principle of charge separation by contact and friction is fundamental to many everyday static electricity phenomena.

sections.title: Charging by Conduction and Induction
sections.narration: Besides friction, charge can be transferred by two other key methods: conduction and induction. Conduction is the most straightforward; it's charging by direct contact. Imagine you have a negatively charged metal sphere and a neutral one. If you touch them together, the excess electrons on the charged sphere, repelling each other, will spread out over the surface of both spheres. When you separate them, both spheres will now have a net negative charge. The original charge has been shared between the two objects. Now, for the more subtle method: induction. Induction is charging without direct contact. Let's say we bring a positively charged rod near a neutral metal sphere, but we don't let them touch. The positive rod will attract the free electrons within the neutral sphere. These electrons will migrate towards the side of the sphere closer to the rod, making that side negatively charged. Consequently, the other side of the sphere, now deficient in electrons, becomes positively charged. The sphere is still neutral overall, but its charge has been polarized. This separation of charge is called induction. We can use this to permanently charge the sphere. While the rod is held nearby, if we connect the sphere to the ground with a wire, electrons from the Earth are attracted by the sphere's induced positive side. These electrons flow up and neutralize that positive charge. If we then disconnect the ground wire *before* removing the rod, the sphere is left with a net excess of electrons. Finally, when we remove the inducing rod, these excess electrons spread out evenly, leaving the sphere with a net negative charge. So, through induction, we charged a neutral object without any contact.

sections.title: Detecting Charge: The Gold-Leaf Electroscope
sections.narration: How can we tell if an object has an electric charge? For this, we can use a simple yet elegant device called a gold-leaf electroscope. It consists of a conducting post with a metal disc or ball on top. At the bottom of the post, inside a protective glass container, two very thin and light leaves of gold foil are attached. When the electroscope is neutral, these leaves hang straight down due to gravity. We can use it in two ways. First, let's use an uncharged electroscope. If we bring a charged object, say a positively charged rod, near the top disc, induction occurs. The rod attracts electrons from the leaves and post up to the disc. This makes the disc negatively charged. Since the leaves have lost electrons, they are left with a net positive charge. Because both leaves are now positive, they repel each other and spread apart, or 'diverge'. The same thing would happen with a negatively charged rod; it would repel electrons down to the leaves, making them both negative, and they would again diverge. So, an uncharged electroscope can detect if an object has charge, but it can't tell us the sign of that charge. To determine the sign, we need a charged electroscope. Let's say we pre-charge our electroscope positively, so its leaves are already diverged. Now, if we bring another positively charged object near the top, it will push even more positive charges from the disc down to the leaves, causing them to repel more strongly and diverge further. However, if we bring a negatively charged object near, it will attract positive charges from the leaves up towards the disc. This reduces the net positive charge on the leaves, causing their repulsion to decrease and the leaves to converge or come closer together. Thus, by observing whether the leaves diverge further or converge, a charged electroscope allows us to determine the sign of an unknown charge.

sections.title: Example: Charging by Friction
sections.narration: Let's walk through a quantitative example of charging by friction. A glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth. After the process, the glass rod acquires a positive charge of +19.2 x 10⁻¹⁹ Coulombs. We have three questions to answer. First, find the number of electrons lost by the glass rod. Second, find the negative charge acquired by the silk. And third, is there a transfer of mass from the glass to the silk? Let's solve this step by step. For part one, we use the principle of charge quantization, q = ne. We need to find n, the number of electrons. So, n = q/e. The charge on the rod is 19.2 x 10⁻¹⁹ C, and the elementary charge 'e' is 1.6 x 10⁻¹⁹ C. Dividing these gives us exactly 12. So, the glass rod lost 12 electrons. For part two, we remember the law of conservation of charge. If the glass rod lost 12 electrons, the silk cloth must have gained those same 12 electrons. Therefore, the charge on the silk is equal in magnitude but opposite in sign to the charge on the glass rod. This means the silk acquires a charge of -19.2 x 10⁻¹⁹ Coulombs. For part three, we consider mass transfer. an electron does have a very small mass, approximately 9 x 10⁻³¹ kilograms. Since 12 electrons moved from the glass to the silk, there was indeed a transfer of mass. The total mass transferred is 12 times the mass of a single electron, which comes out to be 1.08 x 10⁻²⁹ kilograms. This is a negligibly small mass, but technically, mass was transferred.

sections.title: Coulomb's Law
sections.narration: One of the most important pillars of electrostatics is Coulomb's Law, named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb. This law gives us a precise mathematical formula to calculate the force between two stationary point charges. A point charge is an idealized charge whose physical size is negligible compared to the distance between them. Coulomb's Law states that the magnitude of this electrostatic force is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the two charges, q1 and q2. This means if you double one of the charges, the force doubles. If you double both charges, the force quadruples. The law also states that the force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, r, between them. This is a critical 'inverse square law'. If you double the distance between the charges, the force becomes four times weaker. If you triple the distance, the force becomes nine times weaker. The direction of this force is always along the straight line connecting the two charges. It's repulsive if the charges are alike (both positive or both negative) and attractive if they are opposite. Combining these ideas gives us the formula: F = k times the product of q1 and q2, divided by r squared. Here, 'k' is the electrostatic constant, approximately equal to 9 times 10 to the power of 9 Newton-meter-squared per Coulomb-squared. This constant 'k' itself is a shorthand for one over four pi epsilon-naught, where epsilon-naught is another fundamental constant called the permittivity of free space. This formula describes the force when the charges are in a vacuum.

sections.title: Coulomb's Law in a Medium
sections.narration: So far, we've discussed the force between charges in a vacuum. But what happens if the charges are placed in a different material, or medium, like water, oil, or glass? The presence of a medium weakens the electrostatic force between the charges. The formula for Coulomb's law is modified to account for this. The force in a medium is given by F equals q1 times q2, divided by 4 pi epsilon-naught epsilon-r times r-squared. Notice the new term here: epsilon-r, or εᵣ. This is the relative permittivity of the medium, also known as the dielectric constant, often denoted by the letter K. This value is a dimensionless number that tells us how much the medium reduces the electric force compared to a vacuum. For a vacuum or air, K is approximately 1, so the formula is unchanged. But for all other materials, K is greater than 1. For example, water has a dielectric constant of about 80. This means that the electrostatic force between two charges submerged in water is 80 times weaker than it would be in the air at the same distance! For metals, K is considered to be infinite, meaning the electrostatic force inside a conductor is effectively shielded to zero. So, the dielectric constant K is a ratio: it's the force between two charges in a vacuum divided by the force between the same two charges at the same distance in the medium. This effect is crucial in many applications, such as in capacitors, where dielectric materials are used to store more charge.

sections.title: Example: Force in a Dielectric Medium
sections.narration: Let's apply what we've learned about dielectric constants. The force between two point charges placed in a vacuum is 18 Newtons. Now, if a glass plate with a dielectric constant of 6 is introduced between them, what will the new electric force be? This is a direct application of the formula relating force in a vacuum to force in a medium. We know that the force in a medium is equal to the force in a vacuum divided by the dielectric constant, K. In this problem, the initial force in the vacuum, F_vac, is given as 18 Newtons. The dielectric constant of the glass, K or epsilon_r, is given as 6. So, the new force, F_medium, will be 18 N divided by 6. The calculation is simple: 18 divided by 6 is 3. Therefore, the new force between the charges with the glass plate between them is 3 Newtons. The presence of the glass weakened the force by a factor of 6.

sections.title: Example: Superposition on a Line
sections.narration: Let's consider a problem involving multiple charges in a line. Four identical charges, each with a value of +2 microcoulombs, are placed on the x-axis at positions x=0, x=2, x=4, and x=8 centimeters. We need to find the total force exerted on the charge located at x=2 cm. First, let's identify the forces acting on our target charge. The charge at x=2cm is being acted on by three other charges: the one at x=0, the one at x=4, and the one at x=8. Let's analyze the forces from the charges at x=0 and x=4 first. The charge at x=0 is 2 cm away and will exert a repulsive force to the right. The charge at x=4 is also 2 cm away and will exert a repulsive force of the exact same magnitude, but to the left. Because these two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, they will perfectly cancel each other out. The net force from these two charges is zero. Therefore, the only force that we need to calculate is the one exerted by the charge at x=8 cm. This charge is (8 - 2) = 6 cm away from our target charge. Since both charges are positive, this will be a repulsive force, pushing the charge at x=2 cm to the left. We use Coulomb's law to find its magnitude: F equals k times q1 times q2 over r squared. Plugging in the values, we have F = (9x10⁹) * (2x10⁻⁶) * (2x10⁻⁶) all divided by (6x10⁻²)². This simplifies to 36x10⁻³ divided by 36x10⁻⁴, which gives us a force of 10 Newtons, directed to the left.

sections.title: Example: The Smallest Electric Force
sections.narration: Here's an interesting conceptual question: What is the smallest possible electric force between two charges placed at a distance of 1.0 meter? To figure this out, we start with Coulomb's Law: F = k * q1 * q2 / r². We want to find the minimum possible force, F_min. The distance 'r' is fixed at 1 meter, and 'k' is a constant. Therefore, the force will be at its minimum when the product of the charges, q1 * q2, is as small as possible. What is the smallest non-zero charge a particle can have? From our study of charge quantization, we know this is the elementary charge, 'e', which is 1.6 x 10⁻¹⁹ Coulombs. So, to get the minimum possible force, we should place two particles, each with the smallest possible charge 'e', at the given distance. Let's set q1 = e and q2 = e. Now we substitute these values into Coulomb's Law. F_min will be k * e * e / r², which is k * e² / r². Plugging in the numbers: F_min = (9.0 x 10⁹) times (1.6 x 10⁻¹⁹)² divided by (1.0)². This calculates to (9.0 x 10⁹) times (2.56 x 10⁻³⁸), giving a final result of 2.304 x 10⁻²⁸ Newtons. This is an incredibly tiny force, but it represents the fundamental minimum interaction between two charges at a one-meter distance.

sections.title: Coulomb's Law in Vector Form
sections.narration: While the basic formula for Coulomb's law gives us the magnitude of the force, it doesn't explicitly tell us the direction. To handle both magnitude and direction in a single equation, especially in three-dimensional space, we use the vector form of Coulomb's Law. Let's set up a coordinate system. Suppose we have a charge q₁ located at a position described by the position vector r₁-vec, and a second charge q₂ at position r₂-vec. A position vector is simply an arrow drawn from the origin of our coordinate system to the location of the charge. The vector that points *from* charge q₂ *to* charge q₁ is given by the difference r₁-vec minus r₂-vec. The force on charge q₁ due to charge q₂ is denoted as F₁₂-vec. The vector formula is: F₁₂-vec equals k times q₁q₂ divided by the magnitude of the separation vector cubed, all multiplied by the separation vector itself. That is, F₁₂-vec equals (k * q₁ * q₂) / |r₁-vec - r₂-vec|³ times (r₁-vec - r₂-vec). This formula might look more complicated, but it's powerful. The (r₁-vec - r₂-vec) part gives the correct direction—along the line connecting the charges. The cubed term in the denominator ensures the 1/r² magnitude dependence is preserved. Importantly, when using this form, you must include the signs of the charges q₁ and q₂. If q₁ and q₂ have the same sign, their product is positive, and the force F₁₂-vec points in the same direction as (r₁-vec - r₂-vec), which is away from q₂ - a repulsive force. If they have opposite signs, their product is negative, and the force F₁₂-vec points in the opposite direction of (r₁-vec - r₂-vec), which is towards q₂ - an attractive force. The formula automatically handles repulsion and attraction.

sections.title: Example: Force with Position Vectors
sections.narration: Let's work through an example using the vector form of Coulomb's law. We have two point charges, A and B. Charge A is q_A = 1/2 Coulomb and is located at position vector r_A = (i + j + k) meters. Charge B is q_B = 2 Coulombs, located at position vector r_B = (-i - j + 3k) meters. We need to find the force *on* charge A *due to* charge B, which we'll call F_AB. The vector formula is F_AB = k * (q_A * q_B / |r_A - r_B|³) * (r_A - r_B). First, let's calculate the separation vector, r_A - r_B. This is (i + j + k) - (-i - j + 3k). Subtracting the components gives us (1 - (-1))i + (1 - (-1))j + (1 - 3)k, which simplifies to 2i + 2j - 2k. Next, we need the magnitude of this vector. The magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components: sqrt(2² + 2² + (-2)²), which is sqrt(4 + 4 + 4) = sqrt(12). Sqrt(12) can be simplified to 2*sqrt(3). So the magnitude cubed, |r_A - r_B|³, is (2*sqrt(3))³, which is 8 * 3*sqrt(3), or 24*sqrt(3). Now we plug everything into the formula. F_AB = (9 x 10⁹) * (1/2 * 2) divided by (24*sqrt(3)), all multiplied by the vector (2i + 2j - 2k). The charge product is just 1. So we have F_AB = (9 x 10⁹ / 24*sqrt(3)) * (2i + 2j - 2k). We can factor out a 2 from the vector, which cancels with the 24 to make 12. This gives F_AB = (9 x 10⁹ / 12*sqrt(3)) * (i + j - k). Simplifying 9/12 to 3/4, we get a final numerical answer which we can leave in this form.

sections.title: The Superposition Principle
sections.narration: In the real world, it's rare to have only two charges. Usually, a charge experiences forces from many other charges simultaneously. So how do we calculate the total force? The answer lies in a simple but powerful idea called the Superposition Principle. This principle states that the interaction between any two charges is completely independent of the presence of other charges. If you have charges q1 and q2, the force between them is described by Coulomb's law, and that force doesn't change even if you bring a third charge, q3, nearby. The new charge q3 will exert its own force on q1, but it won't alter the original force from q2. Because electrostatic force is a vector quantity, possessing both magnitude and direction, the net force on any single charge is simply the vector sum of all the individual forces exerted on it by every other charge. For example, if we want to find the net force on a charge Q due to other charges q1, q2, and q3, we would first calculate the force vector F1 from q1 on Q. Then we'd calculate the force vector F2 from q2 on Q, and the force vector F3 from q3 on Q. The total or net force on Q is then F_net = F1 + F2 + F3. Remember, this is a vector sum, so you have to add the forces considering their directions, not just their magnitudes. This might involve breaking down forces into their x and y components and adding the components separately.

Because electrostatic force is a vector quantity, possessing both magnitude and direction, the net force on any single charge is simply the vector sum of all the individual forces exerted on it by every other charge.

For example, if we want to find the net force on a charge Q due to other charges q1, q2, and q3, we would first calculate the force vector F1 from q1 on Q. Then we'd calculate the force vector F2 from q2 on Q, and the force vector F3 from q3 on Q.
The total or net force on Q is then F_net = F1 + F2 + F3. Remember, this is a vector sum, so you have to add the forces considering their directions, not just their magnitudes.

sections.title: Example: Charges on an Equilateral Triangle
sections.narration: Let's work on a classic superposition problem. Three equal positive charges, each with charge Q, are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle with side length 'a'. We need to find the resultant force on any one of these charges due to the other two. Let's focus on the charge at the top vertex. This charge will experience two separate forces. The charge on the bottom-left vertex will exert a repulsive force, which we'll call F1, directed upwards and to the right, along the line connecting them. The charge on the bottom-right vertex will exert another repulsive force, F2, directed upwards and to the left. Since all charges are equal (Q) and all distances are the same (a), the magnitudes of these two forces, F1 and F2, will be identical, given by Coulomb's law: F = kQ²/a². Now we need to add these two force vectors. The angle between the two force vectors is the same as the angle of the triangle vertex, which is 60 degrees. We can use the law of cosines for vector addition: F_net² = F1² + F2² + 2*F1*F2*cos(60°). Since F1 = F2 = F, this becomes F_net² = F² + F² + 2*F²*cos(60°). The cosine of 60 degrees is 1/2. So the expression is F² + F² + 2*F²*(1/2), which simplifies to 3F². Taking the square root, we find the magnitude of the net force is F_net = F * sqrt(3). Substituting the expression for F, the final answer is (sqrt(3) * k * Q²) / a². By symmetry, the horizontal components of the forces cancel out, so the resultant force points straight up, away from the base of the triangle.

sections.title: Example: Charges on a Square
sections.narration: Let's analyze the forces in a square configuration. We have four charges, Q, q, Q, and q, placed at the four corners of a square with side length d. The charges are arranged so that like charges are on opposite corners. We want to find the relationship between Q and q such that the net force on one of the 'q' charges is zero. Let's focus on the 'q' charge at the top right corner. It experiences forces from the other three charges. First, the other 'q' charge at the bottom-left corner will exert a repulsive force, F1, along the diagonal. The distance for this force is the length of the diagonal, which is d√2. So, F1 = k * q² / (d√2)². Second, the two 'Q' charges will also exert forces. For the net force on 'q' to be zero, these forces must be attractive, meaning Q and q must have opposite signs. Let's call the force from the top-left Q as F2, and from the bottom-right Q as F3. These are attractive forces. The magnitudes are equal: F2 = F3 = k|Qq|/d². The resultant of these two attractive forces, F2 and F3, which are perpendicular, will be F_resultant = √(F2² + F3²), which is simply F2*√2, and it will point diagonally inwards, exactly opposite to the repulsive force F1. For the net force to be zero, the magnitude of the repulsive force F1 must equal the magnitude of the resultant attractive force. So, F1 = F2√2. Substituting the expressions we found: k * q² / (2d²) = (k|Qq|/d²)*√2. We can cancel k and d² from both sides. This leaves us with q²/2 = |Q|q√2. Dividing by q, we get q/2 = |Q|√2, or |q| = 2√2 |Q|. Since we established that Q and q must have opposite signs for the forces to balance, the final relationship is q = -2√2 Q.

sections.title: Example: Net Force on Charge at Center of Square
sections.narration: Here is another superposition problem. We have a square of side 'd'. Four charges are placed at the corners: Q, 2Q, 3Q, and 4Q, moving counter-clockwise from the top left. A charge 'q' is placed at the very center of the square. We need to find the net force on this central charge q. First, let's establish the distances. The distance from any corner to the center of a square with side 'd' is half the diagonal, which is d/√2. All four charges are at this same distance from the center charge q. Let's define the force from the charge Q on q as F. Because force is proportional to the charge, the force from 2Q will be 2F, from 3Q it will be 3F, and from 4Q it will be 4F. Now let's consider the directions. Assuming Q and q are opposite signs (attractive force), the force F from Q will pull 'q' towards the top-left. The force 2F from 2Q will pull 'q' to the top-right. 3F from 3Q pulls to the bottom-right, and 4F from 4Q pulls to the bottom-left. Now we sum the vectors. Notice that the forces are in opposing pairs. The 3F force to the bottom-right and the F force to the top-left are on the same diagonal. Their resultant is a force of (3F - F) = 2F, pointing towards the 3Q charge (bottom-right). Similarly, the 4F force to the bottom-left and the 2F force to the top-right are on the other diagonal. Their resultant is (4F - 2F) = 2F, pointing towards the 4Q charge (bottom-left). So, we are left with two perpendicular forces, each of magnitude 2F, acting on the charge q. The final net force is the vector sum of these two. Using Pythagoras' theorem, the magnitude is √((2F)² + (2F)²) = √(4F² + 4F²) = √(8F²) = 2√2 F. Finally, we substitute the value of F, which is the force between Q and q: F = kQq / (d/√2)². This is 2kQq/d². So the net force is 2√2 * (2kQq/d²) = (4√2 kQq) / d². The direction is diagonally downwards.

sections.title: Example: Net Force at Center of Hexagon
sections.narration: Let's tackle a problem involving symmetry. Five point charges, each with a value of +q, are placed on five vertices of a regular hexagon of side length L. We need to find the magnitude of the force on a point charge of value -q placed at the center of the hexagon. A direct approach would be to calculate the five force vectors and add them up, which would be quite tedious. Instead, we can use a clever trick based on symmetry. Imagine for a moment that there was a sixth charge, also +q, at the last remaining vertex of the hexagon. What would the net force on the central -q charge be in that case? Each of the six +q charges on the vertices would pull the central -q charge towards it with a force of the same magnitude, F = k * q*q / L², since the distance from each vertex to the center of a regular hexagon is equal to its side length, L. sections.title: Example: Force from a Charged Rod
sections.narration: So far we've dealt with point charges. What if the charge is distributed over an object, like a rod? Let's consider a thin straight rod of length ℓ, carrying a uniformly distributed positive charge q. A positive point charge Q is located on the same line as the rod, at a distance 'a' from the nearest end. We want to find the magnitude of the electric force on the point charge Q. We cannot simply treat the rod's charge 'q' as being at its center, because different parts of the rod are at different distances from Q. This is a perfect problem for integration. We must break the rod down into infinitesimally small pieces, calculate the force from each piece, and then sum up all those forces. Let's define the linear charge density, lambda (λ), which is the charge per unit length: λ = q/ℓ. Now, consider a tiny segment of the rod of length 'dy' at a distance 'y' from the point charge Q. The tiny amount of charge 'dq' on this segment is λ times dy, or (q/ℓ)dy. Since this segment is so small, we can treat it as a point charge. The force 'dF' it exerts on Q is given by Coulomb's law: dF = k * (dq * Q) / y². Substituting for dq, we get dF = (kQq / ℓ) * (dy / y²). All the tiny force elements dF from all the segments of the rod will point in the same direction—away from the rod. So, to get the total force F, we just need to sum, or integrate, all the dF's along the length of the rod. Our integration variable is 'y', the distance from Q. The nearest part of the rod is at y=a, and the farthest part is at y=a+ℓ. So we integrate from a to a+ℓ. The integral of (1/y²)dy is -1/y. Evaluating this from a to a+ℓ gives us (-1/(a+ℓ)) - (-1/a), which is (1/a) - (1/(a+ℓ)). The total force is F = (kQq/ℓ) times [(1/a) - (1/(a+ℓ))]. Combining the fractions gives the final result: F = kQq / (a * (a+ℓ)).

sections.title: Electrostatic Equilibrium
sections.narration: A crucial concept in electrostatics is equilibrium. An object is in electrostatic equilibrium when the net electric force acting on it is zero. This means that all the individual forces from all other charges—all the pushes and pulls—perfectly balance each other out. This point of zero net force is called an equilibrium position. However, there are different kinds of equilibrium, which describe what happens if the charge is slightly disturbed from its equilibrium position. The first type is stable equilibrium. If you displace a charge by a small amount from a stable equilibrium point, it experiences a restoring force that pushes it back towards its original position. Think of a marble at the bottom of a bowl; if you nudge it, it rolls back to the bottom. The second type is unstable equilibrium. If you displace a charge from an unstable equilibrium point, instead of returning, it experiences a force that pushes it even further away. This is like balancing a marble on top of an inverted bowl; the slightest nudge will cause it to roll off and not return. The third type is neutral equilibrium. In this case, if you move the charge a small distance, it feels no force at its new position and simply stays there. It is in equilibrium at the new spot as well. Think of a marble on a flat, level table; you can move it to a new spot, and it will happily stay there. Understanding these types of equilibrium is key to predicting the behavior of charge arrangements.
